items.topic: Śiva binds and frees by svātantrya
items.gist: Śiva veils and reveals himself through his own powers, being both enjoyer, knower, bondage, and liberation.
Those with small intellect trouble themselves over malamaya; the impurity is to be abandoned like dust on crystal.
The vidyaguru speaks of shaktipata, whose intense, medium, and mild forms unfold in graded ways.
Prātibha knowledge is self-arisen and independent of scripture or teacher, though guru excellence increases as dependence decreases.
On the prātibha path there is no need for conventional initiation, vows, or external rites; Mahadeva himself establishes the practitioner.
Prātibha knowledge accomplishes everything; the Triśikā tradition treats self-arisen knowledge as the true initiation.
One who truly knows the tattva is initiated, accomplished, and a yogi, even without ritual procedure.
Pratibhā is the supreme means; the guru who bestows it directly is the giver of boons, and this scripture serves prātibha realization.
Without this teaching one cannot understand the slowness of shaktipata, as explained in the scriptures.
In the Nandishikha dialogue, Śiva teaches that prātibha knowledge is the means, and initiation may occur through it.
The three tattvas are explained through the guru's teaching, leading to prātibha clarity like fire uncovered from ash.
Prātibha knowledge grows through practice, and trans-sensory discrimination makes one turn away from all objects.
